what_its_for: Naloxone is an emergency medicine used to quickly reverse an opioid overdose. Opioids include drugs like heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, and morphine. If someone has taken too much of an opioid, naloxone can block the effects of those drugs and help them breathe normally again. It can save a life in an emergency.
how_to_take: Naloxone comes in different forms: a nasal spray (sprayed into one nostril), an auto-injector (injected into the outer thigh, even through clothing), or a regular injection (given into a muscle, vein, or under the skin by a trained person). For the nasal spray: lay the person on their back, tilt their head back slightly, insert the tip of the nozzle into one nostril, and press the plunger firmly. If the person does not wake up or start breathing normally after 2 to 3 minutes, give a second dose in the other nostril. Always call 911 immediately before or after giving naloxone — it is an emergency medicine, not a substitute for professional medical care.
dosing: The usual adult dose of naloxone nasal spray is one spray (4 mg) into one nostril. If there is no response after 2 to 3 minutes, give another spray in the other nostril. You can repeat this every 2 to 3 minutes if needed until emergency help arrives. For injections, dosing depends on the product and the person's situation — follow the instructions that come with your specific product. Children can also receive naloxone — use the same nasal spray dose for children of any age.
missed_dose: Naloxone is only used in emergencies, not on a regular schedule, so there is no 'missed dose' concern. Keep naloxone with you or nearby at all times if you or someone you know is at risk for an opioid overdose. Replace it right away after it has been used or if it has expired.
storage: Store naloxone at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and freezing temperatures. Do not store it in your car's glove compartment where temperatures can get very hot or very cold. Check the expiration date regularly and replace it before it expires. Keep it in a place where you can find it quickly in an emergency.
what_to_avoid: Do not use naloxone if you are not sure the person is having an opioid overdose — but when in doubt, it is safer to use it, as it will not cause harm to someone who has not taken opioids. Do not leave the person alone after giving naloxone. Because naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes — and opioids may last longer — the person could go back into overdose. Always stay with them until emergency help arrives. Do not give the person more opioids or other drugs after using naloxone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call 911 immediately every time you use naloxone — this is a life-threatening emergency. After an overdose has been treated, the person should be seen by a doctor or go to the emergency room. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist about getting a naloxone prescription if you or someone you know uses opioids, even if prescribed. Ask your doctor about long-term treatment options for opioid use disorder. If you notice the naloxone is not working or you run out of doses, call 911 right away.
when_it_works: Naloxone starts working very quickly — usually within 2 to 5 minutes after it is given. You should see the person start to breathe more normally, wake up, or become more alert. However, naloxone only works for 30 to 90 minutes. Since many opioids last longer than naloxone, the person may go back into overdose after it wears off. This is why calling 911 and staying with the person until paramedics arrive is absolutely critical.
special_populations: Pregnant women: Naloxone can be given to pregnant women during an overdose. The risk of not treating the overdose is far greater than any risk from the medicine. Babies and children: Naloxone is safe for all ages, including newborns. Use the same nasal spray dose. Older adults: Naloxone is safe for older adults. People with opioid dependence: After receiving naloxone, people who are physically dependent on opioids may experience sudden withdrawal symptoms like sweating, shaking, nausea, vomiting, or agitation. This is uncomfortable but not life-threatening. Do not give more opioids to relieve withdrawal — stay calm, keep them safe, and wait for emergency help.
